title: How to Caulk Exterior Windows: Seal the Top, Let the Bottom Drain
metaDescription: Caulking exterior windows takes about 30 to 45 minutes and one tube each: cut out the old bead, seal the top and sides above 40°F, and leave the bottom open.
keywords: how to caulk around an exterior window
do you caulk the bottom trim of an exterior window
how to re caulk outside windows exterior
caulk exterior window trim top, bottom, sides
best way to caulk outside vinyl aluminum windows
how to seal a half moon window
intro:
Caulking exterior windows takes about 30 to 45 minutes and one 10.1 oz tube per window: cut out the old bead, clean and size the joint, then seal the top and side trim joints on a dry day above 40 degrees Fahrenheit and leave the drainage gaps at the bottom open. That last part is where most window caulk jobs go wrong.

Caulk is the outer rain screen on a window, not the whole defense. Behind it sit the nailing flange, flashing tape and the house wrap, all lapped so water runs down and out. Seal the joints that face the weather, keep the exits clear, and the bead you lay this weekend can keep rain out of the wall for years.
quickAnswer: Seal where the side casings meet the siding, the top corners and miters of the trim, the frame-to-trim joint on the top and sides, and the joint above the head trim unless a metal drip cap covers it. Do not seal the underside of the sill, weep slots in vinyl or aluminum frames, or the bottom nailing flange. Remove every failing bead first, use backer rod in gaps deeper than half their width, and push the bead rather than pulling it.

sections.heading: How to Caulk Exterior Windows: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Joint | Seal it? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head trim to siding (above the window) | Yes, unless a drip cap is there | Stops water running behind the trim |
| Side casing to siding | Yes | Takes wind-driven rain |
| Trim miters and top corners | Yes | The most common entry point |
| Window frame to trim, top and sides | Yes | Closes the gap around the unit |
| Sill underside and drip edge | No | Lets trapped water drain out |
| Weep slots in vinyl or aluminum frames | Never | Built-in drainage for the sash track |
| Front or top edge of a metal drip cap | Usually no | Designed to throw water clear |

The job in seven steps:

1. Check the forecast for a dry day above 40 degrees Fahrenheit, with no rain for the caulk's rain-ready window.
2. Cut out every cracked, loose or hardened bead and scrape the joint clean.
3. Clean with a brush, treat mildew, wipe with isopropyl alcohol and let it dry.
4. Probe for soft wood, repair it, and prime bare wood.
5. Push closed-cell backer rod into gaps deeper than about half their width.
6. Tape visible joints, then lay the bead from the top down, pushing the gun.
7. Tool each run at once, pull the tape while wet, and paint after the label's paint window.

### Planning numbers for one window

A typical double-hung window has a trim perimeter of about 18 to 20 feet. One 10.1 oz cartridge lays roughly that much quarter-inch bead, so plan on one tube per window plus a spare for the job. Hands-on time is about 30 to 45 minutes per window, most of it spent removing the old caulk.

sections.heading: Where Do You Caulk Outside Windows?
sections.body:
You caulk the joints that face the weather and leave the drainage paths open. On almost every window that means the top and both sides get sealed, and the bottom gets looked at carefully before anything goes on it.

### Do you caulk all the way around or just across the top?

Neither, exactly. Seal across the top and down both sides, including the miters where the head trim meets the side casings. At the bottom, seal only the joint where the ends of the sill meet the siding on each side, the sill horns, and leave the underside of the sill and its drip edge open. Water that gets behind the trim from a failed bead or a wind-driven storm has to have a way out, and the bottom of the window is that exit.

### Do you caulk the bottom trim of an exterior window?

On a wood sill, do not caulk the underside or the drip kerf. On vinyl and aluminum windows, never caulk or paint over the weep slots in the bottom of the frame; they drain the sash track. On many modern installations the bottom nailing flange is deliberately left unsealed behind the trim so water that reaches the flashing can escape. If you are unsure whether a bottom gap is a drainage path, leave it open.

### What seam on the outside of a window do you caulk first?

Start at the top. Water arrives at the head trim first and gravity drives it into any gap below, so the top corners and the joint above the head trim do the most work. If there is a metal or vinyl drip cap tucked under the siding and lapped over the head trim, leave its front and top edges open. It is meant to shed water outward, and caulking it closed traps water behind it.

### Signs a window needs new caulk

Peeling paint on the trim, dark staining or swelling at the bottom of the casing, a soft sill, or water stains on the drywall under the window all point to failed joints. Find the soft wood before you seal: caulk over rot only hides it.

sections.heading: What Caulk Is Best for Exterior Windows?
sections.body:
Match the sealant to the materials on both sides of the joint and to whether you will paint it.

### Painted wood trim

An elastomeric latex sealant such as DAP Dynaflex 230 or Sashco Big Stretch is the easiest choice. It tools smoothly, cleans up with water, takes paint and stretches far more than plain acrylic, which matters on trim that heats and cools in the sun every day.

### Vinyl windows, vinyl siding and fiber cement

Use a paintable polymer sealant such as OSI Quad. Vinyl moves more than wood with temperature and its smooth face is hard for latex to grip; polymer sealants bond better and come in colors matched to common window and siding finishes.

### Glass, aluminum and unpainted metal

Use 100 percent silicone where the joint will never be painted and takes a lot of water. Silicone cannot be painted, so keep it off trim you plan to coat.

### Brick and stucco openings

Polymer or tripolymer sealants handle porous, alkaline masonry and the large movement between brick and a wood or vinyl frame far better than latex.

### What to skip

Do not use basic acrylic painter's caulk outdoors on window joints. It is cheap and easy to smooth, but most products of that type have very little stretch and crack within a season or two. Look for an ASTM C920 movement class on the label, or at least a product sold as an elastomeric exterior sealant. Our guide to the [best exterior caulk](/best-exterior-caulk/) ranks specific tubes by joint and surface.

sections.heading: What Tools Do You Need to Recaulk Outside Windows?
sections.body:
The kit is short and cheap, and most of it you may already own.

### Removal and prep

- A sharp utility knife or a hooked caulk removal tool
- A stiff putty knife or five-in-one tool
- A wire or stiff nylon brush
- Isopropyl alcohol and clean rags
- Silicone residue remover or mineral spirits if the old bead was silicone
- A diluted bleach solution for mildew, plus a bucket of rinse water
- An awl or screwdriver to probe for soft wood

### Application

- A smooth, dripless caulk gun
- One tube of exterior sealant per window, plus a spare
- Closed-cell backer rod in a few diameters, for deep gaps
- Painter's tape for joints that will be seen
- A plastic tooling spoon, or a cup of water for wet-finger tooling with latex

### Weather you need

Pick a dry spell with surface temperatures comfortably above the label minimum, usually 40 degrees Fahrenheit for latex, and no rain for at least the label's rain-ready time. A mild day is ideal because the joints sit near the middle of their width range, so the new bead is not stretched or squeezed hard in its first weeks. Avoid caulking walls in hot, direct sun, where the bead skins before you can tool it.

If you are unsure how long a given sealant needs before rain, our guide to [how long caulk takes to dry](/how-long-does-caulk-take-to-dry/) lists typical rain-ready and paint-ready windows for each type.

sections.heading: How Do You Remove Old Window Caulk and Prepare the Joint?
sections.body:
Prep takes most of the time and decides how long the new bead lasts. Fresh sealant laid over old caulk bonds only to the old caulk, so when the old bead lets go, both come off together. Remove every failing bead completely.

### Cut out the old bead

Score along both edges of the old caulk with a sharp blade held at a low angle, then hook it out with a removal tool or pull it with pliers. Hardened latex often comes out in chunks; scrape the rest with a stiff putty knife. Go easy on vinyl and soft wood. Old silicone leaves a nearly invisible film that new sealant will not stick to, so scrub those joints with a silicone residue remover or mineral spirits until the surface is clean.

### Clean and dry

Brush out dirt, cobwebs and paint flakes. Treat any mildew with a diluted bleach solution, rinse and let it dry. Wipe both faces of the joint with a rag dampened with isopropyl alcohol to lift dust and oil, then let the joint dry completely. Latex sealants handle damp joints poorly, and every type bonds best to clean, dry surfaces.

### Fix the wood

With the joint open, probe the sill and the bottom of each casing with an awl. If the point sinks in easily, the wood is soft. Small soft spots can be dug out, consolidated and filled with a two-part epoxy product from our [best wood filler](/best-wood-filler/) guide; larger areas mean a new board. Prime any bare wood before caulking.

### Size the joint: the sealant ratio

A sealant joint works best when the bead is about half as deep as it is wide, with a minimum of roughly a quarter inch. For gaps deeper than that, push in closed-cell backer rod about 25 percent wider than the gap so it holds by compression, and seat it evenly with a blunt tool without puncturing it. Backer rod also keeps the sealant from sticking to the back of the joint, so it can stretch between the two sides instead of tearing. For shallow joints where rod will not fit, a strip of bond-breaker tape at the bottom does the same job.

sections.heading: How Do You Apply Caulk Around an Exterior Window?
sections.body:
With the joint clean, dry and sized, laying the bead is the quick part.

### Tape and cut the nozzle

On joints that will be seen, run painter's tape along both sides, leaving just the gap exposed. Cut the nozzle at about 45 degrees, starting small; the opening should be a little narrower than the joint so the sealant is forced in rather than laid on top. Pierce the inner seal and run a short test bead on cardboard.

### Work from the top down

Start at the head trim and work down so you never drag the gun through fresh caulk. Hold the gun at about 45 degrees and push the bead ahead of the nozzle instead of pulling it behind. Pushing packs the sealant into the joint and against both faces. Keep steady trigger pressure and move at a pace that fills the joint with a slight crown, then release pressure at the end of each run so the gun does not ooze.

### Corners, miters and trim joint continuity

The top corners, where the head trim meets the side casings, are the most important spots on the window. Fill the miter first and tool it into the joint, then run the horizontal and vertical beads into it so they overlap. The sealant should be continuous around each corner with no seam or skip, because water follows any break in the line. Take an extra minute on each corner.

### Tool it right away

Tool each run before it skins. Draw a tooling spoon or a wet finger along the bead in one smooth pass, pressing the sealant against both sides and leaving a slightly concave surface. Work in runs short enough to tool within a few minutes, especially with fast-skinning silicone and polymer products, and wipe the tool often.

### Pull the tape while wet

Pull the tape away from the bead at a low angle while the caulk is still wet. If you wait until it skins, the tape tears the edge. Clean smears at once with water for latex or the solvent named on the label for silicone and polymers; cured polymer on vinyl siding is very hard to remove cleanly.

sections.heading: How Do You Caulk Vinyl, Aluminum, Brick and Stucco Windows?
sections.body:
The rules stay the same on every material: seal the weather-facing joints, keep drainage paths open, size the joint and choose a sealant that bonds to both sides. The details change.

### Vinyl windows

Vinyl moves more than wood as it heats and cools, and latex grips its smooth surface poorly. Use a polymer sealant rated for vinyl, in a matching color if it will not be painted. On vinyl-sided houses, do not caulk the J-channel around the window. It is a drainage channel, and sealing it traps water. Seal only where the window or siding instructions call for it.

### Aluminum and steel frames

Clean off oxidation and oil with alcohol first. Use silicone at the glass and a paintable polymer where the frame meets a wall that will be painted. On operable aluminum windows with mitered frame corners, a small amount of sealant at a leaking miter joint is a repair the frame maker may specify; follow their instructions, because some frame joints are part of the drainage path.

### Brick openings

Windows set in brick usually have a wider, irregular gap between the frame or brickmold and the masonry. Wire-brush loose mortar from the edges, use backer rod generously because these gaps run deep, and choose a polymer or tripolymer sealant. Leave the brick weep holes below the window open.

### Stucco

Many stucco walls have a deliberate sealant joint between the stucco and the window frame, sometimes defined by a casing bead. Clean out the old sealant, rod the joint and use a paintable polymer that bonds to cement-based surfaces. Hairline cracks running out from the window corners are a stucco repair, not a caulk job.

### Arched and half-moon windows

A half-moon or arched window follows the same top-and-sides logic, with the whole arc acting as the head. Seal the curved trim-to-siding joint and the frame-to-trim joint around the arc in short runs, tooling each before it skins so the bead follows the curve without gaps. Leave any drainage at the bottom of the unit open.

sections.heading: How Do You Caulk Around an Exterior Door?
sections.body:
An exterior door is caulked much like a window, with the threshold standing in for the sill.

### Seal the brickmold and head

Seal where the brickmold or exterior casing meets the siding on both sides, the top corners and the joint above the head trim, unless a drip cap covers it. Use the same sealant you would on a window: elastomeric latex for painted wood, a polymer for vinyl, fiber cement and masonry.

### Be careful at the threshold

At the bottom, seal the ends of the threshold where they meet the jambs and the siding so water cannot run in at the corners. Do not seal any drainage path the door or sill pan maker built in, such as weep openings at the front edge of a sill pan. When a door is installed over a sill pan, the pan is designed to collect water and send it out the front.

### Check the hardware joints

Look at the joint where the jamb meets the threshold on each side, a common leak point on older doors. Clean it and seal it with a flexible sealant rated for the materials. Weatherstripping and door sweeps handle the gap between the door slab and the frame; caulk does not belong there.

### Order of work

If you are doing windows and doors on the same wall, start at the highest openings and work down. Combine the job with a check of the gutters above: a clogged gutter that overflows over a door or window dumps far more water on the head trim than rain alone, which is one reason [gutter guards](/best-gutter-guards/) help on houses with heavy tree cover.

sections.heading: When Can New Window Caulk Get Rained On or Painted?
sections.body:
Leave the joints alone while they cure. Latex sealants usually skin in under an hour and can take light rain after a few hours, while the core stays soft for days. Polymer and silicone sealants follow their own label times, often faster to a rain-ready skin.

### If rain arrives early

A light shower on a bead that has skinned usually does no harm. A downpour on fresh latex before it skins can wash it out or leave a weak, milky surface. Can you shield new bottom-trim caulk with a plastic drop sheet after a little rain? Yes, as a short-term cover: tape the sheet above the window so it hangs clear of the bead, does not touch it and leaves the sides open so air can still reach the caulk. Once the weather clears, take it down and inspect the bead. Cut out any section that has pulled away or turned chalky and redo it on a dry day.

### Paint

Paint the trim once the label's paint window has passed. Use a quality exterior acrylic and carry the paint a few millimeters onto the bead and onto the siding on each side. Paint shields latex sealant from UV and seals the bond line, where water tries to creep in first. Never paint silicone; paint will not stick to it. If you are repainting porch trim at the same time, the [best porch paint](/best-porch-paint/) guide covers coatings for floors and rails around the door.

### Keeping the seal

Keep sprinklers off the wall for the first day and skip hosing or pressure washing the windows for at least a week. Then check every window in spring and fall for beads that have pulled away from one side, cracked through, hardened or shrunk. Small failures can be cut out and patched; widespread failure means a full redo. A good elastomeric or polymer sealant on a clean, properly sized joint and protected by paint commonly lasts many years. Keep the trim itself sound with paint or one of the finishes in our [best exterior wood sealer](/best-exterior-wood-sealer/) guide.

mistakes.title: Sealing the bottom of the window
mistakes.body: The underside of the sill, the weep slots in vinyl and aluminum frames and the bottom nailing flange on many installs exist to let water out. Caulking them shut traps anything that gets behind the trim, and the sill and framing rot quietly for years. Seal the top and sides and leave the bottom drainage open.

mistakes.title: Laying new caulk over a cracked bead
mistakes.body: It feels faster, but the new caulk only bonds to the old bead, which has already failed. When the old caulk lets go it takes the new layer with it, often within one season. Cut out the old bead, scrape and clean down to bare surfaces, and only then lay fresh sealant.

mistakes.title: Skipping backer rod in deep gaps
mistakes.body: Older wood windows and brick openings often have gaps much deeper than they are wide. Filling them solid wastes tubes, slows the cure and makes a bead too thick to stretch. Push in closed-cell backer rod so the sealant is about half as deep as the joint is wide, then caulk over it.

mistakes.title: Pulling the gun instead of pushing it
mistakes.body: Dragging the nozzle along the joint lays sealant on top of the gap and leaves voids behind it, so the edges fail early. Push the bead ahead of the nozzle at about 45 degrees so the caulk packs into the joint, then tool it at once to press it against both faces.

mistakes.title: Using interior painter's caulk outside
mistakes.body: Basic acrylic painter's caulk is cheap and smooths beautifully, but it has little stretch and breaks down in sun. On window trim that heats and cools every day it usually cracks within a season or two. Use an elastomeric latex or a polymer sealant rated for exterior use and joint movement.

faqs.q: Where do I caulk outside windows?
faqs.a: Caulk the joints that face the weather: where the side casings meet the siding, the top corners and miters of the trim, the joint between the window frame and trim on the top and sides, and the joint above the head trim unless a drip cap covers it. Leave the underside of the sill, weep slots and other drainage gaps at the bottom open.

faqs.q: Do you caulk the bottom trim of an exterior window?
faqs.a: Only partly. Seal the ends of the sill where they meet the siding, but leave the underside of the sill, its drip edge and any weep slots open. Those gaps let water that gets behind the trim drain out. Caulking the bottom closed traps that water against the sill and framing, which is one of the most common causes of hidden rot.

faqs.q: When caulking windows, do you caulk all the way around or just across the top?
faqs.a: Seal across the top and down both sides, and treat the bottom differently. The top and sides face rain and need a continuous bead, especially at the top corners. At the bottom, seal only the sill ends against the siding and leave the drainage paths open, so any water that gets behind the trim can escape.

faqs.q: What is the best way to caulk outside vinyl or aluminum windows?
faqs.a: Use a polymer sealant rated for vinyl, such as OSI Quad, on vinyl frames and siding, and silicone at glass and unpainted aluminum. Remove the old bead, clean with isopropyl alcohol and keep the weep slots in the bottom of the frame open. On vinyl-sided houses, do not seal the J-channel around the window; it is a drainage channel.

faqs.q: Must the old caulk come out before recaulking?
faqs.a: Yes, wherever it has cracked, pulled away or hardened. New sealant laid over old caulk bonds only to the failing material, so both come off together. Cut along both edges, pull and scrape the old bead, and clean the joint. Old silicone leaves a film that blocks adhesion, so scrub it with a residue remover until the surface is clean.

faqs.q: What is the lowest temperature for caulking windows?
faqs.a: Most latex sealants list a minimum of about 40 degrees Fahrenheit for both the air and the surface, and the bead must stay above freezing until it skins. Some polymer and solvent-based sealants are labeled for colder work. Measure the surface temperature on shaded walls and finish early enough that the bead skins before evening dew.

faqs.q: How long does exterior window caulk last?
faqs.a: A quality elastomeric latex or polymer sealant laid in a clean, properly sized joint and protected by paint commonly lasts many years, and many tubes carry long durability claims. Plain acrylic painter's caulk can fail in a few years or less on sunny walls. Check every window each spring and fall and patch failures early, before water reaches the wood.

bottomLine: Caulking exterior windows comes down to a short checklist: seal the top and sides, leave the bottom drainage paths open, cut out the old bead completely, fill deep gaps with backer rod, and push a bead of the right sealant into a clean, dry joint, then tool it straight away. Use elastomeric latex on painted wood, a polymer on vinyl, fiber cement and masonry, and silicone on glass and bare metal. Give it time to cure before rain and paint, then check it every spring and fall. One tube and under an hour per window is cheap protection against rot inside the wall.
